svg.title: The orchestrator handshake and the argument against sub-agents
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure. Four steps run left to right. First, the parent frames a scoped task and names the structured summary it expects back, because free-form prose loses across the boundary. Second, the parent spawns the sub-agent with a fresh minimal context and a maximum number of tool calls, because without the cap a stuck child burns the day. Third, the child runs its own read-think-act loop in isolation and the parent never sees its intermediate tool calls. Fourth, the parent folds only the agreed structure back in, so its window stays small. Below, two panels: the steelman from Cognition in 2025, that sub-agents fragment context so parallel children make locally sensible but globally contradictory edits; and the rule that reconciles the two views — delegate what you could hand to a contractor with a one-paragraph brief and check by output alone, and keep in the main agent anything whose reasoning must stay coherent.
svg.text: The orchestrator handshake, and the case against it
Four steps, and one argument that the boundary should sit further out than most teams put it.
Scope the task and name the
Sub-agents fragment context. A decision made inside one is invisible
to another, so parallel children make locally sensible and globally
contradictory edits, and reconciliation can cost more than the
Delegate work you could hand to a contractor with a one-paragraph
brief and check by its output alone. Keep in the main agent anything
whose reasoning has to stay coherent.
Review sub-agent transcripts on a sample. A summary can hide a skipped test, a hard-coded value, or a file the child should not have touched.
The summaries are what keep the parent's window small, and they are also what makes the child's failures invisible. Both at once.
